- When sentiment is consistently high (≥0.8) over recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast peak by 2–5%.
- If model shows sharp upward spike followed by forecast decline, true price often rebounds — adjust downward peak to match prior trend.
- When sentiment is low (≤0.4) and model forecasts rise, it’s often a false signal — cap upward forecasts at 1–3% above recent mean.
- Model underestimates when sentiment is volatile (alternating 0.4–0.8) — increase forecast by 1–2% to compensate for mean reversion bias.
- For 30-day horizon, model often overcorrects after recent price drops — add 0.5–1.5% buffer to avoid premature recovery.
- If sentiment history shows strong positive momentum (e.g., 3+ consecutive 0.8+), model tends to lag — forecast 1–2 days ahead of true price.
- When sentiment is flat or neutral (0.4–0.6), model often misreads trend — use 3-day moving average of history to anchor forecast.
